According to the World Health Organization (WHO), UNAIDS, and UNICEF recommendations, home-prepared replacement milks for infants of HIV-infected mothers are not suitable in the South African context. These organizations emphasize that commercial infant formula is the only replacement milk that meets all nutritional needs for infants under 6 months.

To provide total nutrition, preparations should include vegetable oils such as soybean oil, which provides essential fatty acids like linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids, and additional vitamins and minerals. The WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF HIV and infant feeding course replacement milk options require revisions to ensure that they meet the nutritional needs of infants.

However, more research is needed to understand how household formulations compare in terms of nutritional content and effectiveness. For instance, studies have shown that intern interns who are in charge of ordering tests for infants on the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) tend to order more arterial blood gases per infant compared to their peers. This may be due to a higher prevalence of unsafe behaviors among these individuals.

In summary, while the WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF recommendations emphasize the use of commercial infant formula, there is limited evidence in South Africa that supports its use for HIV-infected mothers and their infants. Further research is necessary to ensure that replacement milks meet the nutritional needs of this vulnerable population.
